hagl.explanation: "Hagl" means "hail". When you mean the small lead pellets fired from a shotgun, it is also "hagl": "Jægeren lader sit haglgevær med hagl" (The hunter loads his shotgun with pellets).

hakket oksekød.explanation: "Hakket oksekød" means "ground beef". It is built from hakket (chopped) and oksekød (beef). To say ground pork, swap the meat: "hakket svinekød" (ground pork).

hallo.explanation: "Hallo" means "hello". To get someone's attention, say it sharply: "Hallo, hører du efter?" (Hello, are you listening?).

halløj.explanation: "Halløj" means "hey". It is an informal greeting. To greet a friend and ask how things are: "Halløj, hvad så?" (Hey, what is up?).

halm.explanation: "Halm" means "straw". Do not mix it up with "et sugerør" (a drinking straw). To say you drink through a straw: "Jeg drikker med et sugerør" (I drink with a drinking straw).

halv.explanation: "Halv" means "half". It goes before the word it describes: "en halv liter" (half a liter). To say half past the hour on the clock, count toward the next hour: "klokken fire" (four o'clock) is 4:00, but "halv fire" is 3:30, half an hour before four.

halv tre.explanation: "Halv tre" means "half past two". Danish counts halfway toward the next hour, so 2:30 is "halv tre" (halfway to three).

halvanden.explanation: "Halvanden" means "one and a half". To say an hour and a half, put it before "time" (hour): "halvanden time". Before "år" (year) it changes to "halvandet": "halvandet år" (a year and a half).

halvdelen.explanation: "Halvdelen" means "a half". To name the whole that the half comes from, add "af" (of): "halvdelen af pengene" (half of the money). For a measure such as half a liter, use "halv" (half): "en halv liter" (half a liter).

halvvejs.explanation: "Halvvejs" means "halfway". It is built from halv (half) and vej (way). To talk about time: "halvvejs gennem året" (halfway through the year).

ham.explanation: "Ham" means "him". When a man receives the action, use "ham": "Jeg hjælper ham" (I help him). When the man does the action, use "han" (he): "Han hjælper mig" (He helps me). After "med" (with) it is also "ham": "Jeg går med ham" (I am going with him).

han.explanation: "Han" means "he". When a man does the action, use "han": "Han hjælper mig" (He helps me). When the man receives the action, use "ham" (him): "Jeg hjælper ham" (I help him).

handsker.explanation: "Handsker" means "gloves". Do not mix it up with "en vante" (a mitten). To say children wear mittens: "Børnene har røde vanter på" (The children have red mittens on).

hans.explanation: "Hans" means "his". When the owner is a man other than the one doing the action, use "hans": "Peter vasker hans bil" (Peter washes another man's car). To say the man's own, use "sin": "Peter vasker sin bil" (Peter washes his own car).

hardware.explanation: "Hardware" means "hardware". Danish took this word from English and spells it the same way.

hav en god dag.explanation: "Hav en god dag" means "have a good day". To say it as a goodbye and get a reply: "Hav en god dag!" "Tak, i lige måde." (Have a good day! Thanks, you too.) To wish someone a good evening, swap "dag" (day) for "aften" (evening): "Hav en god aften" (Have a good evening).

havearbejde.explanation: "Havearbejde" means "gardening". It is built from have (garden) and arbejde (work). To say you do it, use "at lave" (to make): "Jeg laver havearbejde" (I do gardening).

havre.explanation: "Havre" means "oats". In "havregryn" (rolled oats) and "havremælk" (oat milk), "havre" is the first part of the word.

havregryn.explanation: "Havregryn" means "oatmeal". It is built from havre (oats) and gryn (groats). To name the cooked porridge, say "havregrød" (oatmeal porridge): "Jeg laver havregrød" (I am making oatmeal porridge).

havremælk.explanation: "Havremælk" means "oat milk". It is built from havre (oats) and mælk (milk).

hed.explanation: "Hed" means "hot". Do not mix it up with "varm" (warm), which is milder: "Vandet er varmt" (The water is warm). When the thing described takes "et", add "t": "et hedt bad" (a hot bath).

hej.explanation: "Hej" means "hi". To say goodbye, say it twice: "Hej hej!" (Bye bye!).
